title: Use mathematics to investigate and monitor the financial aspects of personal and community life

lessons.title: Budgets for home and community
lessons.html:
Know where your money goes

A budget is a plan for your money. It shows your income (money coming in) and your expenses (money going out). A budget helps you live within your income and save for the future.

Making a monthly budget

  1. Write down all income: net wage (take-home pay), grants, money from selling eggs or vegetables.
  2. Write down fixed expenses: rent, transport, school fees, funeral policy, loan repayments.
  3. Write down changing expenses: food, electricity, airtime, clothing.
  4. Add up income. Add up expenses.
  5. Income minus expenses = what is left. If it is negative, you spend more than you earn.

Example

ItemAmount (R)
Net wage6 200
Food2 400
Transport900
Electricity and airtime650
School costs500
Funeral policy250
Stokvel500
Total expenses5 200

R6 200 minus R5 200 leaves R1 000. This money can go to savings or an emergency fund.

Community money

Many communities run stokvels and burial societies. Members pay in every month. If 12 members each pay R500 a month, the stokvel collects 12 × R500 = R6 000 each month. Keep written records of every payment and choose honest people to look after the money.

Look at your budget every month. Can you spend less on something? Small savings add up: R20 a week is more than R1 000 a year.

Write your budget on paper or on your phone. Look at it often. Keep slips for big things you buy.

lessons.title: Payslips, VAT and percentages
lessons.html:
Understanding your payslip

Your gross pay is what you earn before deductions. Your net pay is what you get after deductions.

Common deductions

  • UIF: the employee pays 1% of pay, and the employer also pays 1%.
  • PAYE: income tax, if you earn above the tax threshold.
  • Other deductions you agreed to, such as a pension fund or union fees.

Example

Gross pay is R5 800. UIF at 1% = R5 800 × 1 ÷ 100 = R58. If there are no other deductions, net pay = R5 800 − R58 = R5 742.

Working with percentages

A percentage means "out of 100". To find a percentage of an amount: amount × percentage ÷ 100.

  • 10% of R450 = R450 × 10 ÷ 100 = R45.
  • A pay increase of 6% on R6 000 = R360, so the new wage is R6 360.

VAT

VAT (value-added tax) in South Africa is 15%. Many prices in shops already include VAT.

  • A price of R200 without VAT: VAT = R200 × 15 ÷ 100 = R30. Price with VAT = R230.
  • To find the price without VAT from a price that includes VAT, divide by 1.15. R115 ÷ 1.15 = R100.

Comparing prices

A 10 kg bag of maize meal costs R95 and a 5 kg bag costs R52. Price per kg: R95 ÷ 10 = R9.50; R52 ÷ 5 = R10.40. The 10 kg bag is cheaper per kilogram.

Check your payslip every month.

Ask your employer if you do not understand a deduction.

lessons.title: Interest, loans and saving
lessons.html:
Interest

Interest is the price of using money. When you save, the bank pays you interest. When you borrow, you pay interest.

Simple interest

Simple interest = amount × rate × time (in years) ÷ 100.

Example: you save R2 000 at 5% simple interest a year for 3 years. Interest = 2 000 × 5 × 3 ÷ 100 = R300. You will have R2 300.

Compound interest

With compound interest, interest is added to the amount, and next year you earn interest on the interest too.

YearStartInterest at 10%End
1R1 000R100R1 100
2R1 100R110R1 210
3R1 210R121R1 331

Compound interest makes savings grow faster. It also makes debt grow faster if you do not pay.

Loans and credit

  • Always ask for the total cost of a loan: everything you will pay back, including interest and fees.
  • Example: you borrow R3 000 and pay R350 a month for 12 months. You pay back 12 × R350 = R4 200. The cost of the loan is R4 200 − R3 000 = R1 200.
  • Use only registered credit providers. Never give your bank card or SASSA card and PIN to a lender.

Inflation

Prices go up over time. This is called inflation. If bread costs R18 this year and R19.80 next year, the price went up by R1.80, which is 10%. Savings must grow faster than inflation to keep their value.

Key points

  • A budget compares income with expenses; plan to save.
  • Net pay is gross pay minus deductions such as UIF (1%).
  • Percentage = amount × percentage ÷ 100; VAT in South Africa is 15%.
  • Compound interest grows faster than simple interest.
  • Always work out the total cost of a loan.
